THOUGHT: The patient is a 41-year-old woman with two key symptoms: (1) positional dyspnea—specifically worsening when lying on the left side—and (2) an unexplained episode of syncope 10 days prior. Physical exam reveals jugular venous distention (suggesting elevated right-sided filling pressures), a diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border and accentuated in the left lateral decubitus position—a classic auscultatory clue for mitral stenosis or, more specifically in this context, an obstructive left atrial mass impeding mitral inflow. The murmur’s positional accentuation occurs because left lateral decubitus positioning increases venous return to the left atrium and may cause a mobile intracardiac mass (e.g., myxoma) to prolapse into the mitral orifice, creating functional mitral stenosis. Fine crackles and pulmonary congestion on CXR further support elevated left atrial pressure and pulmonary venous hypertension. Critically, the echocardiogram identifies a mass attached to the atrial septum in the left atrium—the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults is atrial myxoma, and ~75–85% arise from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis. Myxomas can cause mechanical obstruction (leading to syncope, dyspnea, orthopnea, or positional symptoms), embolization (though no focal neurologic deficits reported here), or constitutional symptoms (not present here). Syncope in this setting is likely due to transient obstruction of mitral inflow—especially with positional change or vagal triggers—causing acute reduction in cardiac output. The absence of other risk factors (e.g., rheumatic heart disease, prior radiation, malignancy) and the young age make degenerative or congenital etiologies less likely; primary cardiac tumor is the unifying explanation for both the mechanical obstruction (positional dyspnea, diastolic murmur, JVD, pulmonary congestion) and the syncopal episode.

DIAGNOSIS: Left atrial myxoma
